sections.content:
You know the polite imperfect from B2 Unit 2 (*Quería pedirle un favor*, *Venía a preguntar por el horario*, *Llamaba para confirmar la cita*). Pairing that polite imperfect—or an everyday present question—with diminutives lets you **suavizar** ("soften") a request so it sounds warm and unhurried.

In shops, cafés and friendly workplace exchanges, speakers play down the size of what they ask for: *Quería pedirle un favorcito* ("I wanted to ask you a small favour"), *¿Me esperas un momentito?* ("Could you wait for me just a moment?"), *Venía a charlar un ratito* ("I came by to chat for a little while"). Even adverbs take this softening touch: *despacito* ("nice and slowly"), *cerquita* ("nice and close").

Keep register in mind: this double softening (polite imperfect + diminutive) is natural in spoken Spanish—especially across Latin America—but out of place in formal written reports or legal notices.

sections.title: Softening requests with polite imperfect + diminutives
rows: I wanted to ask you a quick little favour. (spoken *cortesía*)
*¿Me esperas un momentito en la esquina?*
Could you wait for me just a moment on the corner?
I came by to talk with you for a little while.
*Camina despacito, que la plaza está cerquita.*
Walk nice and slowly—the square is right nearby.

items.spanish: Disculpe, quería pedirle un favorcito con este documento.
items.english: Excuse me, I wanted to ask you a small favour with this document.

items.spanish: ¿Me esperas un momentito mientras pido el cafecito?
items.english: Could you wait for me just a moment while I order the coffee?

items.spanish: Llamaba para charlar un ratito antes de tu viaje.
items.english: I was calling to chat for a little while before your trip.

items.spanish: Vamos despacito, que la tienda nueva está cerquita de la plaza.
items.english: Let's walk nice and slowly, as the new shop is right near the square.

sections.content: Remember from B2 Unit 2 that the polite imperfect softens your own present wish (*Quería pedirle...*, *Venía a...*), not a completed past story. Combining it with a diminutive adds warmth, never weakness.
